resumen: ## Chronology

**Chronology** is the study of **when** things happened. Events in the correct time order, starting with the earliest, are in **chronological order**. A **timeline** is one of the best ways to show it.
Historians divide time into **periods** with names: the Iron Age, the Middle Ages, Tudor times, Victorian Britain.
## BC and AD
**BC** (or BCE) = before the birth of Jesus Christ. **AD** (or CE) = after his birth. BC years count **down**: 2600 BC is earlier than 776 BC.
## Centuries
Cover the last two numbers and **add one** to the first two: 1348 → 13 + 1 = **14th century**. 1066 → 11th century.
## Periods in this book (1066–1558)
- **The Middle Ages** (medieval period): about **1066 to 1485**. 'Medieval' comes from Latin and means **'middle'** – between the Roman Empire and more modern times.
- **The early Tudor period**: after the Middle Ages. The Tudors were a royal family (Henry VIII, 'Bloody' Queen Mary).
## Key dates

1066 Battle of Hastings · 1070s Tower of London · 1095 Crusades · 1170 Thomas Becket murdered · 1215 Magna Carta · 1265 first parliament · 1283 conquest of Wales · 1337 Hundred Years War begins · 1348 Black Death · 1381 Peasants' Revolt · 1453 Hundred Years War ends (116 years) · 1455 Wars of the Roses · 1485 Henry Tudor (Battle of Bosworth) · 1492 Columbus · 1509 Henry VIII · 1558 Elizabeth I (44-year reign).

temas.titulo: 1.1 · The story of Britain up to 1066
resumen: ## The British Isles
Over **5000** islands off the north-west corner of Europe; fewer than **200** are **inhabited**. The two largest are **Great Britain** and **Ireland**.
## Early settlers

Information comes from **evidence** and **artefacts** (bone, stone, fossils, pottery). Sea level was lower, so a **land bridge** linked Britain to Europe. About **half a million years ago** the first **immigrants** arrived: **hunter-gatherers**. Around **8500 BC** the ice melted, the land bridge disappeared and Britain became an island. About **7000 years ago** people learned to **farm** (wheat, barley, pigs, sheep, goats).
## Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages
Stone Age (tools of wood and stone) → about **2500 BC** the **Beaker people** (decorated pottery) bring metalwork: copper + tin = **bronze** → **Bronze Age** → around **800 BC** iron → **Iron Age**.
## Invaders and settlers
- **Celts** (about 500 BC, central Europe): farmers, druids, Halloween and May Day.
- **Romans** (AD 43, from Italy, about 400 years): roads, towns (Chester, York, Bath), calendars, coins, bricks; words like 'peace' and 'street'.
- **Anglo-Saxons** (from AD 410: Angles, Saxons and Jutes from Denmark and northern Germany): England = 'Angle-land'; words like bed, cat, dog; towns ending -ton, -wich, -ham.

- **Vikings** (late 8th century, from Scandinavia): raided, then settled from 865. **Alfred the Great** of Wessex beat them; the country was split – Viking lands = the **Danelaw**. By the mid-1000s, one king: **Edward**.

resumen: ## Who ruled?

In 1042 England was united under **Edward the Confessor**. He was helped by the **Witan**, a group of advisers. Rich families looked after areas for the king: the heads were **earls** and their land an **earldom**. **Thegns** (pronounced 'thane') were local landowners. Edward also took advice from friends in **Normandy** (northern France).
## People

Population about **1.5 million**. Most worked on the land in small villages. Only about 15 towns had more than 1000 people. Ordinary villagers = **ceorls** ('churl'), some skilled craft workers. Enslaved people = **thralls** (war prisoners, lawbreakers, or people who couldn't pay debts).
## Achievements

Their own **coins** (trade instead of bartering), crafts (the **Alfred Jewel**: 'Alfred had me made'), poetry (**Beowulf**), writing and books (monks wrote **chronicles**), Christian churches, trading ports.
## Why was England a rich prize?
Natural resources: wheat, wool, fish, salt (Cheshire), lead, silver, iron, honey, copper and **tin** (Cornwall supplied most of Europe's tin by 1066).

temas.titulo: 1.3 · Who will be the next King of England?
resumen: **Edward the Confessor** died in **January 1066** (5 January), aged 62, with **no children**. Traditions: the monarch's son, a male relative, the dying king's choice, or the Witan's choice. His great-nephew **Edgar** was only a teenager.
## The Norman – William of Normandy

Duke of Normandy, strong army, fighting family ('William the Bastard'). Edward lived in Normandy 1016–1041; William sent soldiers to help him and claimed Edward **promised him the throne in 1051**. Harold visited William in **1064** and may have promised to support him.
## The Englishman – Harold Godwinson

**Earl of Wessex**. His sister was married to King Edward. Brave, tough soldier (crushed a Welsh uprising in 1063). The only Englishman; the **Witan wanted him**; Edward promised him the kingdom on his **deathbed**.
## The Viking – Harald Hardrada

**King of Norway**, the most feared warrior in Europe ('hard ruler', 'the Ruthless'). Link: a Viking, **Canute**, ruled Norway and England 1016–1035. Supported by **Tostig**, Harold's brother, who wanted revenge.
## Harold's advantage
He was already **in England** and was crowned the very next day (**6 January 1066**).

temas.titulo: 1.4 · Round 1: the Battle of Stamford Bridge
resumen: ## The Viking invasion
- **300 Viking longboats** carry Hardrada's army (with Tostig and about **10,000 Vikings**) up the **Humber Estuary** and River Ouse. They land on **18 September 1066**.
- **20 September**: earls **Morcar and Edwin** attack with about 3500 men and are defeated at the **Battle of Fulford**, near York.
- The Vikings take **York**, with hostages and supplies to be delivered at **Stamford Bridge**.
## The Battle of Stamford Bridge – 25 September 1066

Harold marched over **300 km in four days** from London. The Vikings were surprised; many had **taken off their armour**. One Viking blocked the bridge (killed 40 English) until an English soldier **floated under the bridge** and stabbed him. **Hardrada was killed** (arrow) and **Tostig** too. Harold won: the Vikings only needed **24 ships** to go home.
## Bad news
Harold heard that **William of Normandy had landed near Hastings**.
## Writing an account
An **account** is a story about the past in **chronological order**, full of facts and dates, in the **third person** and **past tense**.

temas.titulo: 1.5–1.6 · The armies and the Battle of Hastings
resumen: ## William lands (1.5)

On **28 September 1066**, three days after Stamford Bridge, **William landed at Pevensey**, on the south coast. He brought over **300 ships**, about **10,000 soldiers** and **2000 horses**. He moved along the coast to **Hastings**, burning villages, and **rested** for several days with plenty of supplies.
## Harold's army: two groups

- **Housecarls** (about **2500**, but up to half killed at Stamford Bridge): the backbone of the army – well paid, fully trained, finest weapons. Favourite weapon: a huge **battleaxe** (handle over a metre, razor-sharp iron blade). Helmets, chain mail, large **round shields**; they locked shields to form a **shield wall**. Killing power 9, defence 9, speed 1, range 1.

- **Fyrd** (pronounced 'fird', **over 6000**): not as experienced or well equipped. Leaders had swords and javelins; most used **farming tools** such as **pitchforks and scythes**. Fighting on their **home turf**. Killing power 3, defence 5.
## William's army: three units
- **Knights** (about **2000**): highly trained, on horseback, **chain mail** (hauberk), kite-shaped shields, spears, swords and **maces**.
- **Archers** (about **1500**): 6–7 arrows a minute, could kill from about 180 m; very little armour.
- **Foot soldiers**: the main part, metre-long swords and kite-shaped shields.
## The Battle of Hastings – Saturday 14 October 1066
- Harold's tired army marched **400 km**. On **13 October** he placed it on top of **Senlac Hill**, with **streams and boggy areas** on both sides.
- The Normans carried a **flag from the Pope**.
- **9am**: arrows bounced off the **shield wall**; foot soldiers and knights could not break it.
- A **rumour** said William was dead – he lifted his helmet: 'Look at me! I am alive'.
- About **3pm**: **fake retreats** – the English chased the Normans down the hill and were cut down by the knights. The archers fired again.
- At **sunset Harold was killed**. William buried him secretly, although Harold's mother offered his weight in **gold**.

temas.titulo: The new King: William the Conqueror
resumen: After winning the Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066), **William of Normandy** became the new King of England.
- He was **crowned on Christmas Day, 25 December 1066**, in **Westminster Abbey**, London.
- He became known as **William the Conqueror**. The **Norman Conquest** was the last time England was invaded and taken over by a foreign power.
- Harold and many of his key followers were dead; the land was **divided among William's Norman followers**.
- England's **language, rulers and way of life changed forever** (the new rulers spoke Norman French).
- The Normans built **castles** to control England – work began on the **Tower of London** in the **1070s**.
- His half-brother **Bishop Odo** ordered the **Bayeux Tapestry** (1070s).
- In **1086** William ordered the **Domesday Book**, a survey of England. He died in **1087**.

puntos: To keep the English under control

temas.titulo: 1.7 · How did King Harold die? (sources and accounts)
resumen: ## Sources and interpretations
- A **source** is created **at the time** you are studying (a letter, a cartoon, a painting from the period).
- An **interpretation** is made **much later** (a book, film, article) by someone who has reviewed the sources and wants to show a particular opinion.
## The evidence
- **Source A** – Guy of Amiens (before 1068): four **knights** killed Harold – lance in the chest, head cut off, cut open with a javelin, leg hacked off.
- **Source B** – William of Jumièges (1070, Norman monk): Harold fell 'in the first shock of battle'.
- **Source C** – William of Poitiers (around 1070, Norman priest): just says the king had been killed.

- **Interpretation D** – the **Bayeux Tapestry** (1070s, 70 m long, ordered by **Bishop Odo**): 'Harold Rex Interfectus Est' = 'Here King Harold has been killed', above a man with an **arrow in his eye**.
- **Interpretation E** – Amatus of Montecassino (**1080**): first written record of the **arrow in the eye**.
- **Interpretation F** – William of Malmesbury (around 1125): arrow in the brain, then a knight hacked his thigh.
- **Interpretation G** – Simon Schama (2000).
Most of the evidence is **Norman** – there is no Anglo-Saxon account.
## Writing a narrative account (causation)

Show **causes** (why) and **consequences** (results). Steps: **Plan** → **Check order and add detail** (dates!) → **Write your story** → **Make links** with **connectives** (as a result of this, because of this, then, meanwhile, finally…).

resumen: The key words from Chapter 1 (in bold red in the book; meanings in the glossary).
- **artefact** – an object made by people in the past · **evidence** – information that helps us find out about the past
- **immigrant** – a person who comes to live in a country · **inhabit** – live in a place · **hunter-gatherer**
- **century** – 100 years · **chronology** – the study of when things happened
- **Witan** – the king's advisers · **earl / earldom** · **thegn** – local landowner · **ceorl** – ordinary villager · **thrall** – enslaved person

- **monarch** – a king or queen · **Pope** – head of the Catholic Church · **monk** – lives in a monastery · **chronicle** – a monk's official diary · **archaeologist** – studies the past by digging up remains
- **invasion** – entering a country by force · **housecarl** · **fyrd** · **mace** · **chain mail** · **lance** – a long spear used by a knight
- **source** – evidence from the time · **interpretation** – a later view of the past
